subtype: Pained and tearful in adult life [Mismatch]
passage: You looked worried when you saw me dab my eyes at the retirement lunch, Irfan. Sit, I'll tell you something. I'm Manjula, thirty years in this accounts office, and at twenty-five I cried at this very desk. My father's surgery had gone well that morning; the call came at eleven, after a week of night shifts at the hospital. The relief just spilled out. Mr Bhalla from audit walked past, saw my face and marched to our manager to complain that someone had been harsh with me. Only Lakshmi from payroll came over, set down a cup of tea and asked, "Good tears or bad ones? Do you want company, or shall I shut the door?" I said, "Good. Door, please." She closed it and left me alone for ten minutes. Today at the lunch, my tears were gratitude and a little grief at leaving. You couldn't have known that by looking, so thank you for asking me instead of guessing.

qa.q: What news came at eleven on the day Manjula cried at the desk?
qa.a: The call said Manjula's father's surgery had gone well that morning.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when the tears came at twenty-five, and how else were they read?
qa.a: Manjula felt deep relief after a week of fear and tiring night shifts, so they were good tears; Mr Bhalla read the same tears as hurt from a harsh manager.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped most, and why?
qa.a: Lakshmi's question helped most: she asked what kind of tears they were and offered company or a shut door, so Manjula could choose instead of being guessed about.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt about Mr Bhalla's complaint, and what would have changed if he had asked first?
qa.a: The manager may have felt accused of something they never did; if Mr Bhalla had asked Manjula first, he would have learned the tears were relief and skipped the complaint.

grounding: Shows that a young adult's tears at work can come from relief rather than hurt, and that asking and offering privacy is more respectful than guessing.

subtype: Contemptuous and disgusted in relationships and work [Regulating]
passage: At the Johannesburg studio where Hana designs packaging, the third late file from Thabo landed at 5:40 on a Friday. She felt her lip curl before she had read a line. Typical. Can't he manage one deadline? Her fingers were already typing a reply with "AGAIN??" in the subject line. She stopped, deleted it, and said under her breath, "That's contempt talking." She took her coffee up to the rooftop, watched the minibus taxis crawl along the street below and let her jaw unclench. On Monday she asked Thabo for ten minutes. "The last three files came in after five, and it's meant weekend work for me. Can we look at what's getting in the way?" Thabo rubbed the back of his neck. "The client sends changes at four. I've been too embarrassed to push back." They drafted a two o'clock cut-off together, and Hana found she could look him in the eye again.

qa.q: What time did Thabo's third late file land?
qa.a: It landed at 5:40 on a Friday.

qa.q: What does Hana's curled lip and the "AGAIN??" subject line suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Most likely contempt and frustration at Thabo after more weekend work, though end-of-week tiredness could also have sharpened her reaction.

qa.q: What small step helped Hana before she replied?
qa.a: She named the feeling as contempt, deleted the harsh draft and took a break on the rooftop, so on Monday she could raise the late files calmly.

qa.q: How might Thabo have felt if the "AGAIN??" email had gone out on Friday?
qa.a: He would likely have felt attacked and even more embarrassed, and might have kept hiding the four o'clock client changes instead of admitting them.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult catching contempt toward a colleague, pausing, and then raising the concern with respect.

passage: Past midnight at a small hotel in Osaka, Tariq slammed his phone on the counter. "I paid for this room three weeks ago! Where is it?" Aiko, twenty-four and alone on the night desk, felt her heart kick. She took a half step back and let her voice drop lower than his. "You've had a long trip, and this isn't what you expected. Let me look." The booking had been cancelled by the website, not the hotel. She didn't argue about whose fault it was. "I can ring two hotels nearby right now, or you can sit in the lounge while I check." Tariq leaned over the counter, shouting. Aiko stepped further back and pressed the button for the duty manager. "I want to help you, and my colleague is coming to help too." When Mr Sato arrived, Tariq sank onto the sofa, rubbing his eyes. Twenty minutes later he had a room across the street.

qa.q: What did Aiko offer to ring for Tariq?
qa.a: She offered to ring two hotels nearby right now.

qa.q: How can you tell Aiko was frightened, and why did she keep her voice low?
qa.a: Her heart kicked and she stepped back, so she was likely scared, though the step back may also have been trained habit; she dropped her voice on purpose so Tariq's anger had nothing to match.

qa.q: What went right when the calm approach stopped working?
qa.a: When Tariq leaned over shouting, Aiko moved further away and called the duty manager, putting safety first instead of handling it alone.

qa.q: What might Tariq's rubbing his eyes on the sofa suggest about his night?
qa.a: It suggests Tariq was exhausted after a long trip, and his fury may have covered worry about having nowhere to sleep.

grounding: Shows a young adult lowering their voice, keeping distance and offering a calm way out, then getting help when calm alone is not enough.

subtype: Apologetic and guilty in adult responsibility [Regulating]
passage:
Tuesday, 11 pm. Jeevan's notes to self.
Messed up today. I copied the wrong delivery date into the client email, the 18th instead of the 8th, and Farhan spent two hours on the phone untangling it. My first draft of a message to him said "sorry sorry, I'm hopeless, I ruin everything." Deleted it. That's not an apology, that's asking him to comfort me.
What I actually sent: "Farhan, I put the wrong date in the Mehta order and it cost you your afternoon. I've called the client, confirmed the 8th in writing, and I'll add a date check to my sending list. I'll take the Thursday follow-up calls so you get that time back."
He replied: "👍 happens, thanks for sorting it."
Stomach still feels tight. But the fix is done, and I don't need to keep punishing myself tonight. Tomorrow: date check before every send.

qa.q: Which date did Jeevan put in the client email by mistake?
qa.a: Jeevan put the 18th instead of the 8th.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan delete the first draft, and what was Jeevan feeling?
qa.a: Jeevan felt guilty and ashamed, and saw that "I'm hopeless" would make Farhan do the comforting; the tight stomach shows the guilt lingered, though late-night tiredness may add to it.

qa.q: What made Jeevan's second message a good apology?
qa.a: It named the exact mistake and what it cost Farhan, showed the repair already done, and offered the Thursday calls, so the amends matched the harm.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt if he had received the first draft instead?
qa.a: He might have felt he had to reassure Jeevan on top of fixing the order, leaving him more drained than helped.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult naming a work error, apologising specifically and repairing it without sliding into over-apology or self-blame.

subtype: Shy, embarrassed and ashamed in adult settings [Regulating]
passage:
Monday: Pranav's microphone squealed during the quarterly town hall, and in the scramble he called the finance head by the wrong name. A ripple of laughter went round the room. His ears burned for the rest of the day, and at lunch he carried his dal-rice to his desk instead of the canteen.
Thursday: In the team huddle he kept his camera off and typed "agree" in the chat rather than speak. Gurleen messaged him afterwards: "I once called our CEO 'Mummy' in a review 😅 Nobody remembers. Chai at four?" Over chai she told the whole story, and he laughed for the first time that week.
The next Tuesday: Pranav asked one question in the smaller design review. His voice wobbled, but nobody looked up oddly. On Friday he gave a three-minute update, stumbled once, said "let me try that again," and carried on.

qa.q: What did Pranav type in the huddle chat instead of speaking?
qa.a: Pranav typed "agree" in the chat.

qa.q: What do Pranav's burning ears and lunch at his desk suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Most likely embarrassment and shame after the laughter, though he might also have just wanted quiet to recover from a stressful morning.

qa.q: What small step would help someone like Pranav after a public mistake?
qa.a: Starting with one question in a smaller meeting, as Pranav did, lets the fear shrink before a bigger task like a full update.

qa.q: Why might Gurleen have shared her own embarrassing story?
qa.a: Gurleen probably wanted Pranav to see his slip as ordinary; showing she had lived through something similar made it easier for him to laugh 😊

grounding: Shows a young adult withdrawing after a public mistake and easing shame through a supportive colleague and small, gradual steps.

subtype: Thoughtful, interested and doubtful in meetings [Interpreting]
passage: Disha had eight minutes left in the room before the sales team took it over, and the projector kept flickering. She rushed through her plan to move client onboarding online. Across the table, Gautam raised his eyebrows at the third slide and started writing fast in his notebook. When she asked, "Thoughts?" he said only, "Okay." Her stomach dropped. He hates it, she thought, and he's listing everything wrong. The door handle turned; sales was early. Disha held up a hand to them, "Two minutes, sorry," and turned back. "Gautam, you reacted at the timeline slide. I'd rather hear it now than guess. What stood out?" He looked up, surprised. "Honestly? I was copying your checklist for my team. But eight weeks feels tight. Could we talk about twelve?" Disha let out a breath. Half of what she had feared was wrong, and the other half was a fair point.

qa.q: How many minutes did Disha have left in the room?
qa.a: Disha had eight minutes left before the sales team took the room.

qa.q: What was Disha worried about when Gautam said only "Okay"?
qa.a: Disha felt anxious that Gautam hated the plan and was listing faults, though his raised eyebrows and fast notes could just as well have meant interest, which was partly true.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Gautam directly about the timeline slide, even with sales at the door, worked because it swapped guessing for his real view: interest plus one fair doubt.

qa.q: How might Gautam have seen the meeting if Disha had walked out without asking?
qa.a: Gautam might have thought his "Okay" said enough and never raised the eight-week worry, leaving a problem to surface later.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional reading raised brows, fast notes and a short reply, then asking for views because the cues alone prove nothing.

subtype: Surprised, relieved and worried at work [Interpreting]
passage: At 10:15 the whole floor of the Gangtok insurance office went quiet as the email landed: the claims unit would shrink by four posts, and the rural outreach pilot was approved. Dolma glanced across at Ganga. Ganga's eyes went wide, then she let out a long sigh and pressed her palms flat on the desk. When the supervisor passed, Ganga said, "All good, all good," in a voice pulled tight as wire. Dolma's mind ran ahead: was Ganga's post one of the four? Or was that sigh relief, since the pilot was Ganga's idea? She didn't ask in front of everyone. At the tea break she waited until they were alone by the window. "That email was a lot. How are you taking it?" Ganga laughed shakily. "Both ways. My pilot got through, and I'm thrilled. But my cousin is in claims, and I've no idea if she's safe." Dolma nodded and passed her the biscuit tin.

qa.q: How many posts would the claims unit lose?
qa.a: The claims unit would shrink by four posts.

qa.q: What did Ganga's wide eyes and long sigh most likely show, and what else could they have meant?
qa.a: They showed surprise and mixed feelings: Ganga was thrilled about the pilot yet worried for her cousin in claims; before asking, Dolma could just as easily have read them as fear for Ganga's own post.

qa.q: What made Dolma's check-in work?
qa.a: Dolma waited for a private moment and asked an open, calm question instead of guessing, so Ganga could explain both feelings 🙏

qa.q: How might the supervisor have read Ganga's "All good, all good"?
qa.a: The supervisor may have taken the words at face value and believed Ganga was fine, missing the worry in the tight voice.

grounding: Shows a young professional reading a colleague's wide eyes, sigh and tense voice at mixed news, and using a calm check-in to learn the cause.

subtype: Deadpan and impassive as professional style [Mismatch]
passage: Vikas, you asked why I never tell juniors to smile more. Sit, and I'll tell you. When I was twenty-four and new at the pathology lab, the others called me "Stone-face Rehana." My first supervisor had said, "Keep your face still; patients read everything." So I did. Good results, bad results, a birthday cake in the staff room: same face. Some colleagues decided I was bored. My manager praised my calm. Both were partly guessing. That winter I was also doing night classes and sleeping four hours, and the blank face was holding a lot in. Mrs Fernandes, the senior technician, watched for a few weeks. Then one evening she said, "Your face hasn't changed in a month, but you've reread the same slide label three times. Are you all right, or is this just how you work?" I told her everything. She didn't ask me to smile. She helped me swap two late shifts.

qa.q: What nickname did Rehana's colleagues use at the pathology lab?
qa.a: They called Rehana "Stone-face Rehana."

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling behind the still face that winter?
qa.a: Rehana was exhausted and strained from night classes and four hours of sleep, though colleagues read the same face as boredom and the manager read it as calm.

qa.q: Which choice by Mrs Fernandes made the difference, and why?
qa.a: She watched the pattern for weeks, noticed the reread slide labels, and asked directly without demanding a smile, so Rehana could explain and get two late shifts swapped.

qa.q: Why might the colleagues who thought Rehana was bored have reacted differently if they had known about the night classes?
qa.a: They would likely have felt sympathy instead of distance, and might have offered help rather than judging the blank face.

grounding: Shows that a blank, even manner at work can mean composure, boredom or hidden strain, and that patterns and direct questions reveal which.

subtype: Detached, weary and neutral at work [Interpreting]
passage:
Subject: Checking in (no need to reply today)

Hi Neelam,

This is a slightly awkward email, so bear with me. For the last two weeks you've seemed quieter in stand-ups: short answers, camera off, no jokes about the office printer. On Tuesday I heard myself tell Rohit in the pantry that you were "totally burnt out." I had no business saying that, and I'm sorry. I don't actually know. You might be deep in the audit, unwell, dealing with something at home, or maybe this is just a heads-down season for you.

So instead of guessing, I'm asking: how are you doing? If you want to talk, I'm free for a walk at lunch any day this week. If you'd rather not, that's completely fine too, and I'll keep my pantry opinions to myself. 🙂

Take care,
Nirmala

qa.q: What did Nirmala tell Rohit in the pantry on Tuesday?
qa.a: Nirmala said Neelam was "totally burnt out."

qa.q: Why did Nirmala write this email, and what was Nirmala feeling?
qa.a: Nirmala felt guilty about labelling Neelam to Rohit and concerned about the quiet stand-ups, while knowing the quietness might only mean a busy audit or a heads-down season.

qa.q: What could Nirmala have said to Rohit instead on Tuesday?
qa.a: Nirmala could have said, "I don't know, I'll ask," and then checked in with Neelam directly rather than offering a label.

qa.q: What would it be like for Neelam to hear from Rohit that colleagues think Neelam is burnt out?
qa.a: Neelam might feel talked about and exposed, especially if the quiet was only focus on the audit, and could trust the team less.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional noticing a coworker's flat, quiet manner and choosing kind curiosity over a label.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
subtype: Culture and gender norms about visible reactions [Mismatch]
passage: At Yara's farewell lunch in a Toronto engineering firm, the team gathered round a lopsided cake. When Kaito stood to thank her for two years of mentoring, his face went bright red and his voice stayed flat. "Look at Kaito, furious we're losing her," someone joked. Yara, meanwhile, was crying openly, dabbing her eyes and laughing. In her family, tears at goodbyes were expected, a sign of respect. In Kaito's, his dad had always said a man keeps his face steady at work. A new intern whispered, "Guess she's the emotional one and he's the robot." Later, by the coat rack, Yara didn't guess. "Your face went red during the speech. Were you embarrassed, or upset about something?" Kaito shrugged, then smiled. "Mostly embarrassed. I hate speeches. And sad, honestly. I just don't show it the way you do." Yara hugged the cake box. "Both work," she said.

qa.q: Which city was Yara's farewell lunch in?
qa.a: It was in Toronto, at an engineering firm.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling when his face went red during the speech?
qa.a: Kaito felt embarrassed about speaking and sad about Yara leaving; the joke read the red face as fury, showing how easily a flush is misread.

qa.q: What would you advise the intern who called them "the emotional one" and "the robot"?
qa.a: Drop the labels, since families teach different rules about crying, and ask people how they feel, as Yara did by the coat rack.

qa.q: How might Yara see Kaito's flat voice differently after their talk?
qa.a: Yara now knows the flat voice hid sadness too, so she can see it as a different family style rather than coldness.

grounding: Shows how family and gender norms shape crying and blushing, and that asking a person beats stereotyping their visible reaction.
